title: Troubleshooting Services & Networking
summary: Step through a broken Service: existence, DNS, spec, endpoints, Pods, kube-proxy, then debug CoreDNS itself.

blocks.text: A caller dials a port number (Service) and nobody answers. The investigator works outward, one layer at a time: do the bays answer directly? Does the number exist? Is a fence (NetworkPolicy) in the way? Does the phone directory know the name? Does the raw number work? Is the spec right? Does the switchboard list any bays (EndpointSlices)? Is the switchboard operator (`kube-proxy`) on duty? Test from a throwaway bay with a shell.
A Service gives no response. Work through these in order; each step rules out a layer.

rows: Each Pod answers on the port you expect
Not `NotFound`. Forgetting to create it is common
Review ingress rules on the target Pods
on the node: `ps auxw | grep kube-proxy`, its logs, iptables/IPVS rules

blocks.text: To see what a Pod sees, start a throwaway shell, or exec into an existing Pod:

kubectl run -it --rm --restart=Never busybox --image=registry.k8s.io/busybox:1.27.2 sh
kubectl exec <pod-name> -c <container-name> -- <command>

`kubectl expose deployment <deployment-name> --port=<port> --target-port=<container-port>` creates a Service for a Deployment. `--port` is the Service port and `--target-port` is where the Pods listen.

If the short name fails in the phone directory, dial more of the address: `<service-name>.<namespace>`, then the full `svc.cluster.local` form. If only the yard-qualified name works, you're calling from another yard. If only the full address works, check the bay's dialing card (`/etc/resolv.conf`): its `nameserver` must be the directory's number, and its `search` list must include the yard suffixes. If even `kubernetes.default` fails, debug the directory itself.
If the short name fails, try wider names. The suffix is `<namespace>.svc.<cluster-domain>`, usually `cluster.local`.

nslookup <service-name>                               # same namespace only
nslookup <service-name>.<namespace>
nslookup <service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
nslookup kubernetes.default                           # should always work
cat /etc/resolv.conf

items: Short name fails but the namespace-qualified name works: the client is in another namespace. Use the cross-namespace name.
FQDN works but relative names don't: check the Pod's `/etc/resolv.conf`.
`nameserver` must be the cluster DNS Service IP (given to the kubelet by `--cluster-dns`).
`search` must include `<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`, `svc.cluster.local` and `cluster.local` (the domain comes from `--cluster-domain`).
`options ndots:5` is the Kubernetes default, so search paths are used for its names.
If even `kubernetes.default` fails, debug the DNS Service itself, or kube-proxy.

blocks.text: Check the number's settings like a switchboard engineer: is the dialed port listed, does `targetPort` match where the bays actually listen, is it a number rather than a string, and is the protocol right? If the switchboard lists no bays (`ENDPOINTS <none>`), the number's tag filter (`spec.selector`) doesn't match the bays' coloured tags, often a typo or `app` versus `run`. Compare with `kubectl get pods -l`.

items: Is the port you call listed in `spec.ports[]`?
Does `targetPort` match the port the Pods actually listen on?
Numeric port written as a number (`9376`), not a string (`"9376"`)?
Named `targetPort`? The Pods must expose a port with that same name.
Is the protocol right?

blocks.text: An EndpointSlice with `ENDPOINTS <none>` means the Service's `spec.selector` doesn't match the Pods' `metadata.labels`. A typo, or a different label key such as `app` vs `run`, is the classic cause. Compare with:

items: Ready Pods with a high **RESTARTS** count can cause intermittent failures.
When testing Pods directly, use the **Pod** port (`targetPort`), not the Service port.

blocks.text: If the number exists, lists bays, and the bays answer, suspect the switchboard operator (`kube-proxy`). Is it running on the ship? Do its routing rules mention your Service, in iptables or IPVS mode? Its logbook should say `Setting endpoints` for your Service; if not, restart it with `-v` set to 4. A bay that can't call itself through its own number points to hairpin mode on the cargo officer (`kubelet`).
If the Service exists, has endpoints and the Pods answer, suspect the proxy layer. These apply only if your cluster uses kube-proxy.

ps auxw | grep kube-proxy                 # running on the node?
iptables-save | grep <service-name>      # iptables mode
ipvsadm -ln                              # IPVS mode
curl <cluster-ip>:<port>                 # from the node

items: Logs: a file such as `/var/log/kube-proxy.log`, or `journalctl`, depending on the node OS. Errors contacting the control plane suggest a node config problem.
The log line `Using iptables Proxier` shows the mode. The other common mode is `ipvs`.
iptables mode: one `KUBE-SERVICES` rule per Service port, a `KUBE-SVC-<hash>` chain, and a `KUBE-SEP-<hash>` chain per endpoint.
IPVS mode: a virtual server per Service port, with a real server per Pod endpoint.
Look for `Setting endpoints for <namespace>/<service-name>` in the logs. If it's missing, restart kube-proxy with `-v` set to 4.

blocks.text: A Pod that can't reach **itself** through its own Service IP points to hairpin mode. The kubelet's `--hairpin-mode` must be `hairpin-veth` or `promiscuous-bridge`.

When the phone directory (CoreDNS) itself is suspect, send a test bay (`dnsutils`) to look up `kubernetes.default` and read its dialing card. Then check the directory staff: are CoreDNS Pods running, any odd lines in their logs, does the `kube-dns` Service exist with endpoints? CoreDNS keeps the old `kube-dns` name. The `log` plugin records every lookup, and `SERVFAIL` may mean CoreDNS lacks the badge to list services and endpointslices.
Create the `dnsutils` test Pod from the docs example, then:

kubectl exec -i -t dnsutils -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl exec -ti dnsutils -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl get pods --namespace=kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl logs --namespace=kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl get svc --namespace=kube-system
kubectl get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=kube-dns --namespace=kube-system

rows: Problem with CoreDNS or its Services. Keep going
The DNS add-on may not be deployed; deploy it
Suspicious messages point at config or upstream problems
See the endpoints section of Debug Services

items: CoreDNS keeps the label `k8s-app=kube-dns` and the Service name `kube-dns` for backward compatibility.
To see each query, add the `log` plugin to the Corefile: `kubectl -n kube-system edit configmap coredns`. Changes can take a minute or two to reach the Pods.
`SERVFAIL` for Service names? Check `kubectl describe clusterrole system:coredns -n kube-system`. CoreDNS needs list/watch on services and endpointslices.
A query without a namespace only searches the Pod's own namespace. Use `<service-name>.<namespace>`.

blocks.text: A few directory problems are well known. On Ubuntu, systemd-resolved can swap in a stub dialing card that sends calls in a loop; point the kubelet's `--resolv-conf` at the real file (kubeadm does this for you). glibc reads only 3 nameservers and Kubernetes needs one of them, so extras get dropped. Alpine 3.17 or earlier may lose DNS answers over 512 bytes; use 3.18 or later.

items: **systemd-resolved** (for example, Ubuntu) replaces `/etc/resolv.conf` with a stub that can cause a forwarding loop. Point the kubelet's `--resolv-conf` at `/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf`. kubeadm detects this and sets it for you.
glibc allows only **3** nameserver records, and Kubernetes needs 1 of them. Extra entries get dropped. dnsmasq or `--resolv-conf` can help.
Alpine **3.17 or earlier** may fail DNS answers over 512 bytes (no TCP fallback). Use 3.18 or later.

questions.stem: `wget -O- hostnames` from a Pod fails with 'unable to resolve host address'. What does the guide tell you to check first?

options.text: Whether the Service exists: kubectl get svc hostnames
options.explanation: A missing Service is the first thing to rule out.
Proxy rules come much later in the flow.
Only for a Pod reaching itself through its Service.
Pointless if the Service doesn't exist.

questions.stem: `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web` shows ENDPOINTS `<none>`, but the Pods are Running. What's the most likely fault?

options.text: The Service selector doesn't match the Pod labels
options.explanation: The EndpointSlice controller selects Pods by the Service's spec.selector.
kube-proxy doesn't build EndpointSlices.
DNS doesn't decide endpoints.
That affects name lookups, not endpoint selection.

questions.stem: `nslookup web` fails from a Pod, but `nslookup web.prod` works. What's going on?

options.text: The client Pod is in a different namespace than the Service
options.explanation: Short names only search the Pod's own namespace.

options.text: The cluster DNS Service is down
options.explanation: The qualified lookup worked, so DNS is up.
The namespace-qualified name resolved, so the guide points to a namespace mismatch, not endpoints.
The proxy mode doesn't affect DNS search paths.

questions.stem: Your Service resolves and has endpoints, but connections fail. Which checks of the Service spec does the guide list? Select 3.

options.text: targetPort matches the port the Pods listen on
options.explanation: Listed.

options.text: A named targetPort matches a port name exposed by the Pods
options.explanation: Listed.
Listed.

options.text: The Service type is not ClusterIP
options.explanation: The walkthrough's working Service is a ClusterIP Service.
Not on the guide's checklist; the example uses None.

questions.stem: True or false: When you test Pods directly (bypassing the Service), you should use the Service port rather than the Pod's port.

options.explanation: Direct tests use the Pod port (targetPort, 9376 in the example).
Correct. The Service port only applies when going through the Service IP.

questions.stem: Which line in a Pod's /etc/resolv.conf must point at the cluster DNS Service?

options.explanation: It is set from the kubelet's --cluster-dns.
search lists domain suffixes.
Controls when search paths are tried.

questions.stem: In iptables mode, which chain should exist once per Pod endpoint of a Service?

options.explanation: One SEP chain per endpoint.
Holds one rule per Service port, shared by all Services.
One per Service port; it jumps to the SEP chains.

questions.stem: Which command lists the CoreDNS Pods?

options.explanation: CoreDNS keeps the kube-dns label for compatibility.
The label value is kube-dns.
Lists Services, not Pods.
Wrong label and wrong namespace.

questions.stem: `nslookup kubernetes.default` fails from the dnsutils Pod. Which are documented next steps? Select 3.

options.explanation: Look at nameserver and search.

options.text: Check that CoreDNS Pods are Running
options.explanation: No Pods means DNS isn't deployed.

options.text: Check that the kube-dns Service has endpoints
options.explanation: Use kubectl get endpointslice for kube-dns.
Not a step on the DNS debugging page.
Not a documented step.

questions.stem: CoreDNS logs `SERVFAIL` for internal Service names. Which documented check fits?

options.text: Check that ClusterRole system:coredns allows list/watch on services and endpointslices
options.explanation: CoreDNS needs those permissions to resolve Service names.
SERVFAIL here points at CoreDNS permissions, not the Service IP.
Not a documented fix.
Not a documented fix.

questions.stem: Where is the CoreDNS Corefile stored, and how do you edit it?

options.text: ConfigMap coredns in kube-system: kubectl -n kube-system edit configmap coredns
options.explanation: Shown when adding the log plugin.
That's the host resolver config.
The Corefile lives in a ConfigMap.
That holds permissions, not configuration.

questions.stem: True or false: On nodes using systemd-resolved, kubeadm automatically adjusts the kubelet to use the correct resolv.conf.

options.explanation: Correct. It points the kubelet at /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf.
The page says kubeadm detects systemd-resolved and adjusts the kubelet flags.

questions.stem: A Pod can reach a Service from other Pods but not through its own Service IP. In iptables mode with a bridge network, what should you check?

options.text: The kubelet's effective hairpin mode (hairpin-veth or promiscuous-bridge)
options.explanation: Hairpin traffic needs one of these.
Other Pods reach it, so endpoints are fine.
This is an IP-level problem.
Unrelated to Service IP traffic.

questions.stem: Which kubectl command creates the Service in the guide's walkthrough?

options.explanation: Service port 80 forwards to Pod port 9376.
Ports reversed: the Pods listen on 9376.
Creates the Deployment, not the Service.
Scales the Deployment.
